prompt_free_text:
This paper studies sample efficiency in safe reinforcement learning and proposes ESPO, a primal-style method that combines a three-mode update rule with adaptive sample-size manipulation based on reward-cost gradient conflict. The central idea is intuitive: when reward and safety gradients conflict, use more samples to reduce uncertainty and stabilize the update; when they align, use fewer samples. The paper also claims convergence guarantees in a tabular setting and empirical gains on Safety-MuJoCo and Omnisafe.

Overall, I find the paper interesting and potentially valuable, especially because adaptive sampling is underexplored in safe RL and the proposed conflict-aware criterion is a natural fit for constrained optimization. The empirical results suggest that the method can improve reward and safety while reducing training time and total samples. However, I also have substantial concerns about clarity, consistency, novelty relative to PCRPO, and the strength of the theoretical and empirical evidence supporting the specific adaptive sampling mechanism. My assessment is therefore mixed: the paper has a promising idea, but in its current form it does not yet fully substantiate several of its main claims.

The main strength of the paper is the problem it targets. Sample efficiency is indeed a major bottleneck in safe RL, and most existing on-policy safe RL methods do use fixed rollout budgets per iteration. The paper identifies a plausible reason why fixed budgets are suboptimal: the difficulty of the update depends on whether reward and safety objectives are aligned or conflicting. This is a sensible observation, and using gradient conflict as a signal for adaptive sampling is conceptually appealing. I also appreciate that the method is built on top of a recognizable optimization structure, namely the three-mode framework inherited from PCRPO, which makes the proposal easier to interpret.

A second strength is that the paper attempts to connect algorithm design, theory, and experiments. The authors do not merely propose a heuristic but also provide convergence statements and propositions about reduced oscillation and sample efficiency. Even if I have reservations about the current form of these results, the effort to provide formal grounding is commendable. The empirical section is also reasonably broad in that it includes both primal and primal-dual baselines and evaluates on two benchmark suites.

That said, the paper’s presentation has several serious issues. The most immediate one is inconsistency in the headline empirical claims. The abstract appears twice, and the two versions report different sample-efficiency gains: one says “5–9% fewer samples,” while the other says “25–29% fewer samples.” This is not a minor typo because sample efficiency is one of the paper’s central contributions. The discrepancy undermines confidence in the reported results and needs to be resolved everywhere in the paper. More generally, the manuscript contains many grammatical errors, duplicated text, formatting artifacts, and notation issues. These do not by themselves invalidate the work, but they make it harder to assess and suggest the paper is not yet polished enough for publication.

A more substantive concern is novelty. The optimization backbone appears to be PCRPO’s three-mode framework, and the main new ingredient is adaptive sample size selection based on gradient conflict. That may still be publishable if convincingly justified, but the paper should be much clearer about what is genuinely new algorithmically versus inherited from PCRPO. In particular, the update rules in the soft-constraint region are essentially PCRPO-style gradient manipulation, while the sample manipulation itself is described only at a high level through equations of the form X + X zeta_t^+ or X + X zeta_t^-. The paper does not clearly specify how zeta_t^+ and zeta_t^- are computed in practice, whether they are bounded, how sensitive performance is to them, or how they depend quantitatively on the gradient angle or other statistics. Without this, the core contribution feels underspecified. If the practical algorithm is deferred to the appendix, the main text still needs to summarize the exact adaptive rule.

Relatedly, there seems to be a possible mismatch in Section 4.3 between the gradient-angle cases and the corresponding update equations. In Section 4.1, equation (3) is used when theta_{r,c} > 90 degrees and equation (4) when theta_{r,c} <= 90 degrees. But in Section 4.3, the textual description appears to swap these associations in the bullet points for soft constraint violations. If this is not a typo, it is a serious algorithmic inconsistency; if it is a typo, it still needs correction because it affects reproducibility and interpretation.

The theoretical section is ambitious but not fully convincing in its current presentation. Theorem 4.1 gives a convergence rate in a tabular softmax setting, but from the main text it is not clear how much of this result depends on the adaptive sampling mechanism itself, as opposed to the underlying three-mode update structure. In fact, the theorem seems to establish essentially the same rate as CRPO, and the paper explicitly notes this. That is acceptable if the adaptive sampling improves constants or practical efficiency, but then the theory should isolate what is gained specifically by sample manipulation. Proposition 4.3, which is supposed to establish sample efficiency, is stated only qualitatively: ESPO “needs fewer number of samples” than the version without sample manipulation to meet target gaps. This is too weak as a theoretical contribution. A meaningful sample-complexity result should quantify the reduction under explicit assumptions and characterize the dependence on conflict frequency, variance, or the adaptive schedule. As written, the proposition reads more like a claim than a sharp theorem.

Similarly, Proposition 4.2 on reduced oscillation depends on “adaptively choosing” the parameters x_t^r and x_t^c, but the paper does not explain whether such choices are constructive, computable online, or merely existential. If the proposition requires idealized choices that are not what the implemented algorithm uses, then its practical relevance is limited. The theory section would benefit from a much clearer separation between what is proved for the actual algorithm and what is shown under additional assumptions or idealized parameter choices.

Another issue is the gap between theory and experiments. The theory is for tabular CMDPs with softmax policies and apparently natural policy gradient style updates, whereas the experiments are on deep continuous-control benchmarks. Such theory-to-practice gaps are common in RL, but then the paper should be careful not to overstate the guarantees. Phrases like “theoretically guarantees convergence, optimization stability, and improved sample complexity bounds” are too strong given that the practical setting is far outside the theorem’s assumptions and the sample-complexity proposition is not quantitatively explicit.

The empirical evaluation is promising but still leaves important questions unanswered. The reported sample savings are based on total samples consumed until training ends, but it is not fully clear whether all methods are compared under matched stopping criteria, matched wall-clock budgets, and matched implementation optimizations. Since ESPO dynamically changes sample counts, one needs to know whether baselines were allowed early stopping once they reached similar reward/safety levels, or whether they were simply run for a fixed maximum budget while ESPO terminated earlier. If the latter, the comparison is less compelling. A stronger evaluation would report reward and cost as functions of environment interactions and wall-clock time, plus the sample count needed to reach predefined reward and safety thresholds.

The paper also claims reduced training time by 21–38%, but training time in RL can depend heavily on implementation details, parallelism, hardware, and framework overhead. The authors briefly acknowledge this, but the current evidence is still insufficient. For time comparisons to be meaningful, the paper should specify hardware, number of parallel environments, whether gradient computations for reward and cost are shared across methods, and whether ESPO incurs extra overhead from computing gradient angles and adaptive schedules. Since PCRPO already computes both gradients, the incremental overhead may be small, but this should be documented.

The baseline selection is reasonable, but the fairness of comparison needs more detail. ESPO is built on a primal framework and compared against both primal and primal-dual methods across different benchmark suites. However, the paper itself notes that Safety-MuJoCo primarily supports primal methods and Omnisafe is more favorable to primal-dual methods. This split makes cross-paradigm conclusions harder to interpret. It would help to include ESPO and all relevant baselines within the same codebase and benchmark wherever possible, with matched architectures and hyperparameter tuning effort. In particular, because adaptive sampling changes the number of trajectories per iteration, hyperparameters such as learning rate, batch normalization of advantages, and update epochs may need retuning for fairness.

The ablation section is too underdeveloped in the main text. Since the adaptive sampling rule is the main novelty, the paper should prominently include ablations on: fixed larger batch size, fixed smaller batch size, monotonic batch increase schedules, variance-based adaptive sampling, and angle-threshold variants. Right now, it is difficult to tell whether the gains come from the conflict-aware criterion specifically, from simply using fewer samples overall, or from the underlying PCRPO-style update rule. A particularly important control would be a version of PCRPO with the same average sample budget as ESPO but allocated uniformly, to test whether adaptivity itself matters. Another useful ablation would vary the conflict threshold from 90 degrees to other values or use a continuous function of cosine similarity rather than a binary split.

I also think the paper should better justify why gradient angle is a reliable proxy for sample need. Conflict indicates directional disagreement, but sample complexity is more directly tied to estimator variance and signal-to-noise ratio. In noisy policy-gradient settings, the estimated angle itself may be unstable, especially with small batches. This creates a chicken-and-egg issue: one uses the estimated conflict to decide the batch size, but the estimate of conflict may itself require sufficient samples. The paper should discuss this explicitly and ideally provide empirical evidence that the angle estimate is stable enough to drive adaptation. For example, reporting the distribution of estimated angles across seeds and iterations, or comparing angle estimates under different batch sizes, would strengthen the argument.

There are also some conceptual ambiguities around safety. The paper often says ESPO “ensures safety,” but the experiments seem to evaluate expected cost relative to a threshold during training. In safe RL, there is an important distinction between expected cumulative constraint satisfaction and per-trajectory or per-step safety during exploration. The method appears to address the former, not the latter. The wording should be more precise to avoid overstating the safety guarantee.

Despite these concerns, I do think the paper has potential. The idea of conflict-aware adaptive sampling in safe RL is plausible and could be impactful if properly developed. The empirical trends, assuming they are correct and consistently reported, suggest that the method may indeed reduce wasted interactions while improving optimization behavior near the safety boundary. The reduced-oscillation intuition is also appealing and aligns with known difficulties in constrained policy optimization.

To strengthen the paper, I would recommend the following concrete revisions. First, fix all inconsistencies and presentation issues, especially the contradictory abstract claims and the apparent equation mismatch in Section 4.3. Second, clearly specify the adaptive sampling rule in the main text: how zeta_t^+ and zeta_t^- are computed, clipped, initialized, and tuned. Third, sharpen the theory so that the contribution of sample manipulation is explicit and quantitative; if only qualitative statements are possible, tone down the claims accordingly. Fourth, expand the empirical analysis with stronger ablations and fairer sample-efficiency metrics, including threshold-reaching curves and matched-budget comparisons. Fifth, analyze the robustness of the gradient-conflict signal under noisy gradient estimates. Sixth, clarify the exact notion of safety being guaranteed and avoid implying stronger guarantees than the theory supports.

My overall recommendation is borderline to weak reject in the current form, mainly because the core novelty is underspecified, the theoretical claims are not yet sufficiently sharp, and the empirical evidence does not fully isolate the contribution of adaptive sampling. However, I view the underlying idea as promising. With a cleaner presentation, a precise adaptive rule, stronger ablations, and more careful theory/claim alignment, this could become a solid contribution.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes Efficient Safe Policy Optimization (ESPO), a primal-based safe RL method that augments a PCRPO-style three-mode update scheme with adaptive sample-size manipulation based on reward-cost gradient conflict. The method increases samples when reward and safety gradients conflict and decreases them otherwise. The paper claims theoretical guarantees on convergence, reduced oscillation, and improved sample efficiency, and reports empirical gains on Safety-MuJoCo and Omnisafe benchmarks in reward, constraint satisfaction, sample usage, and training time.
strengths: Addresses an important problem in safe RL: improving efficiency while maintaining constraint satisfaction.
The core intuition—using reward/safety gradient conflict to adapt sampling effort—is reasonable and potentially useful.
Builds on an existing primal framework and introduces a simple, implementable modification rather than a highly complex pipeline.
Includes both theoretical and empirical sections, and evaluates on multiple benchmark suites with comparisons to primal and primal-dual baselines.
Empirical results suggest the method can reduce wall-clock training time and total environment interactions relative to fixed-sample baselines.
weaknesses: The paper has multiple internal inconsistencies that undermine credibility, including contradictory abstract claims about sample-efficiency gains (5–9% fewer samples vs. 25–29% fewer samples).

The algorithm description appears inconsistent: in Section 4.1, Eq. (3) is for conflicting gradients and Eq. (4) for aligned gradients, but Section 4.3 swaps these assignments when describing the practical algorithm.

The theoretical claims about sample efficiency are vague and not quantitatively established in the main text; Proposition 4.3 states ESPO needs fewer samples than a version without sample manipulation, but no explicit sample complexity bound or conditions are given.

The theory is developed only for a tabular softmax/NPG setting, whereas experiments are in deep continuous-control benchmarks; the gap between theory and practice is substantial and not adequately discussed.

The empirical evaluation lacks sufficient detail in the provided text: number of seeds, variance/error bars, statistical significance, exact stopping criteria, and how adaptive sample counts are implemented are unclear.

Comparisons may be unfair if ESPO is allowed to terminate earlier or use fewer samples while baselines are run with fixed budgets; the paper does not clearly separate gains from early stopping versus better learning dynamics.
The claimed safety improvements are not rigorously substantiated in the provided text with aggregate violation metrics, confidence intervals, or standardized evaluation criteria.
The method introduces additional hyperparameters (soft thresholds h-, h+, sample adjustment factors zeta_t^+, zeta_t^-) but there is limited discussion of sensitivity, tuning burden, or robustness.
methodological_flaws: There is a scientific-logic inconsistency in the practical algorithm description: Section 4.3 assigns Eq. (3) to the case theta<=90 and Eq. (4) to theta>90, which contradicts Section 4.1 where Eq. (3) is explicitly for theta>90 and Eq. (4) for theta<=90. This raises concern that either the algorithm or its description is incorrect.

The sample-manipulation rule in Eqs. (6)–(7) is underspecified. The signs/magnitudes of zeta_t^+ and zeta_t^- are not constrained in the main text, so the claim that one rule increases samples and the other decreases them is not mathematically guaranteed as written.

The convergence theorem does not appear to establish any benefit from adaptive sampling over the underlying fixed-sample method; it only matches CRPO-like rates. Thus the main novelty (sample manipulation) is not theoretically tied to the stated convergence improvement claims.

Proposition 4.3 is too weak to support the headline claim of improved sample complexity bounds. It provides only a qualitative comparison ('needs fewer samples') without an explicit bound, rate, or dependence on problem parameters, making the claim of provable sample-complexity advancement insufficiently justified.

The oscillation-reduction proposition relies on adaptively choosing mixing parameters x_t^r and x_t^c, but the paper does not clearly specify how these are chosen in practice or whether the required choice is computationally feasible and consistent with the implemented algorithm.

Empirical validity is weakened by inconsistent reporting of sample-efficiency gains between the two abstracts and by the absence, in the provided text, of uncertainty estimates and statistical testing. This makes it difficult to assess whether the reported improvements are robust.

The fairness of empirical comparisons is questionable because baselines appear to use fixed total sample budgets while ESPO reports lower sample counts to reach some endpoint, but the endpoint criterion is not clearly standardized across methods.

The theory assumes exact or sufficiently accurate gradient information in a tabular setting, yet the method's key decision variable is the estimated gradient angle under stochastic sampling. The paper does not analyze how noisy angle estimation affects mode switching, safety, or sample adaptation in practical deep RL.
